units.title: Unit 19 — Families
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 42–43 (PDF pages 46–47).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
learningObjectives: Distinguish nuclear, extended, immediate and close-knit families, and use appropriate expressions for different types of relatives.
Describe family circumstances sensitively with conventional collocations for marriage, separation and home life.
Use verbs naturally when speaking about pregnancy, children, childcare responsibilities and custody.
Avoid frequent verb errors such as begin a family, get children and wait a baby; recognise formal or potentially judgemental expressions.

items.example: A nuclear family may consist of two parents and their children.
items.note: The term refers to the parents-and-children unit, in contrast to an extended family.

items.example: Her extended family includes grandparents, uncles, aunts and cousins.
items.note: Extended family includes relatives outside the immediate parents-and-children unit.

items.example: We invited only close relatives to the small wedding.
items.note: Close relatives usually include parents, siblings and children; close may describe degree of kinship.

items.example: I have distant relatives in another part of the country.
items.note: Distant refers to a less immediate family connection, not necessarily geographical distance.

items.pt: primo de segundo grau; prima de segundo grau
items.example: At the reunion I met a second cousin I had never seen before.
items.note: A second cousin shares great-grandparents with you; not the same as a first cousin.

items.example: Lucia is a distant cousin whom I only meet at family reunions.
items.note: Distant indicates a relatively remote family connection; it does not imply living far away.

items.pt: sua família imediata; seus familiares mais próximos
items.example: Please tell your immediate family about the change in plans.
items.note: Immediate family generally means your closest family members, such as parents, partner, children or siblings; definitions vary by context.

items.pt: família unida; família com laços próximos
items.example: They are a close family and meet for dinner every weekend.
items.note: Here close describes the strength of emotional relationships rather than degree of kinship.

items.example: Growing up in a close-knit family gave him a strong support network.
items.note: Close-knit emphasises strong family bonds and frequent mutual support.

items.example: She was raised in a loving family that encouraged her interests.
items.note: Describes a family whose members show affection and care.

items.example: He grew up in what the town considered a respectable family.
items.note: Respectable often refers to social approval and reputation, not necessarily healthy private relationships.

items.example: The novel explores the tensions within a dysfunctional family.
items.note: Describes problematic or unhealthy patterns of family interaction; it can sound judgemental in everyday conversation.

items.example: Although they are not blood relatives, they have always treated each other as family.
items.note: A blood relative is related by birth rather than through marriage or another social relationship.

items.section: B · Marriage, separation and home life
items.example: She keeps photographs of her late husband on the bookshelf.
items.note: Late before a spouse or family member means deceased; it is respectful and does not mean unpunctual.

items.section: B · Marriage, separation and home life
items.example: He often talked about the kindness of his late wife.
items.note: Late means that the wife has died; the same adjective is used with husband.

items.pt: marido afastado; marido com quem se está separado
items.section: B · Marriage, separation and home life
items.example: Her estranged husband now lives in another city.
items.note: Estranged is relatively formal and indicates that the relationship has broken down, even if divorce has not occurred.

items.pt: esposa afastada; esposa com quem se está separado
items.section: B · Marriage, separation and home life
items.example: He remains in occasional contact with his estranged wife.
items.note: Estranged describes a difficult or broken relationship, not the death of a spouse.

items.section: B · Marriage, separation and home life
items.example: The couple agreed to a trial separation before making any permanent decision.
items.note: A trial separation is a period of living apart while considering the future of the relationship.

items.section: B · Marriage, separation and home life
items.example: They decided to get a divorce after several years apart.
items.note: Get a divorce is the standard everyday expression; do a divorce is not idiomatic.

items.pt: divórcio litigioso; divórcio marcado por ressentimentos
items.section: B · Marriage, separation and home life
items.example: Their bitter divorce affected the whole family.
items.note: Bitter suggests anger, conflict and resentment surrounding the separation.

items.pt: divórcio conflituoso; divórcio marcado por hostilidade
items.section: B · Marriage, separation and home life
items.example: The couple went through an acrimonious divorce involving several legal disputes.
items.note: Acrimonious is more formal than bitter and suggests intense hostility or argument.

items.section: B · Marriage, separation and home life
items.example: She is on friendly terms with her ex-husband.
items.note: Ex-husband refers to a former husband after a marriage has ended, not a husband who has died.

items.section: B · Marriage, separation and home life
items.example: He and his ex-wife share responsibility for their children.
items.note: Ex-wife means a former wife following divorce, rather than a late wife.

items.pt: lar desfeito; família marcada por separação ou ruptura
items.section: B · Marriage, separation and home life
items.example: He disliked being described as coming from a broken home.
items.note: A traditional expression for a household disrupted by separation or divorce; it may sound judgemental and is not proof of poor parenting.

items.section: B · Marriage, separation and home life
items.example: The charity aims to help every child grow up in a stable home.
items.note: Stable refers to reliable living conditions and emotional security, not a particular family structure.

items.pt: lar com privações; ambiente familiar de grande carência
items.section: B · Marriage, separation and home life
items.example: The programme supports children growing up in deprived homes.
items.note: Deprived highlights a lack of resources or adequate living conditions, not necessarily a lack of love.

items.section: B · Marriage, separation and home life
items.example: His friends call him a confirmed bachelor because he has no plans to marry.
items.note: Traditionally describes a man who seems determined to remain unmarried; it may sound old-fashioned.

items.pt: constituir família; começar a ter filhos
items.example: They hope to start a family once they have settled into their new flat.
items.note: Start a family often means have a first child; begin a family is not the usual expression.

items.example: They want to have children in the future.
items.note: Use have children, not get children, for becoming or being parents.

items.example: They are expecting a baby at the end of the year.
items.note: Expect a baby means be pregnant or anticipate the birth; waiting for a baby is not the natural expression here.

items.pt: ter um bebê; dar à luz um bebê
items.example: She had a baby in March and is enjoying her parental leave.
items.note: Have a baby can refer to giving birth; get a baby is not appropriate in this meaning.

items.pt: o bebê está previsto para nascer; o parto está previsto
items.example: The baby is due in early December.
items.note: Due describes the expected time of birth; it does not guarantee the baby will arrive on that date.

items.pt: mãe ou pai que cria os filhos sem companheiro(a)
items.example: As a single parent, he manages childcare and work on his own.
items.note: A single parent may be divorced, widowed or unmarried; single does not always mean never married.

items.pt: mãe solo; mãe que cria os filhos sem companheiro(a)
items.example: She returned to university while working as a single mother.
items.note: Single mother is a woman raising a child without a partner; it does not necessarily imply divorce.

items.pt: criar uma criança; educar um filho
items.example: It can be challenging to raise a child while working night shifts.
items.note: Raise means care for a child as they grow; grow up is what the child does.

items.example: Her grandparents helped bring up the children.
items.note: Bring up means raise or care for children; the object is the child, not the person doing the growing up.

items.pt: criar uma família; criar os filhos
items.example: They raised a family in a small town near the coast.
items.note: In the sense of bringing up children, raise a family is especially common in American English.

items.pt: solicitar a guarda; pedir judicialmente a guarda
items.example: The father decided to apply for custody of his daughter.
items.note: Apply for custody of a child means formally request the legal right or responsibility to care for them.

items.example: The court may grant custody to one parent or arrange shared care.
items.note: Grant custody is a formal legal phrase; give custody is a less formal alternative.

items.example: The judge decided to give custody of the children to their aunt.
items.note: Give custody is a natural alternative to the more formal grant custody.

items.pt: sustentar sua família; prover o necessário à família
items.example: She works hard to provide for her family without sacrificing all her free time.
items.note: Provide for means support financially or supply essential needs; for is required.

items.pt: estabelecer um lar; começar a morar por conta própria
items.example: The couple set up home in a small rented house.
items.note: Set up home means establish a household, usually when starting independent domestic life.

sectionsChecked: A · Family relationships: nuclear and extended families, relatives, relationships, marriage and types of homes
B · Parents and children: starting a family, pregnancy, child-rearing, custody, financial support and independent living

units.title: Unit 20 — Relationships
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 44–45 (PDF pages 48–49).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Topics: People and relationships · friendship and romantic relationships
learningObjectives: Use conventional verb–noun collocations to describe making, strengthening, maintaining and damaging friendships.
Distinguish close or mutual friends from casual acquaintances and talk naturally about keeping or losing contact.
Describe falling in love, affection, commitment and proposals using complete conventional expressions.
Recognise figurative wording and learner errors such as find friends, make a friendship and have a relation with someone.

items.example: It is easier to make friends when you join a club or community group.
items.note: Make friends is the normal expression; find friends is not the preferred collocation for creating friendships.

items.example: She struck up a friendship with a neighbour at a local concert.
items.note: Strike up is a phrasal verb suggesting the beginning of a friendship, sometimes unexpectedly.

items.pt: estabelecer uma amizade; criar uma amizade
items.example: They formed a friendship during their first year at university.
items.note: Use form a friendship, not make a friendship; the emphasis is on establishing the relationship.

items.example: The colleagues gradually developed a friendship outside work.
items.note: Develop a friendship highlights the way a relationship grows over time.

items.example: Their lasting friendship began when they were neighbours as children.
items.note: Lasting suggests that a friendship continues for many years.

items.example: Working together on the project helped cement their friendship.
items.note: Cement is a metaphor meaning make an existing relationship stronger, not begin one.

items.pt: estragar uma amizade; prejudicar uma amizade
items.example: A dispute over money can spoil a friendship.
items.note: Spoil a friendship means damage its quality; it contrasts with cement a friendship.

items.pt: uma amizade se fortalece; uma amizade cresce
items.example: A friendship grows when both people make time for each other.
items.note: Grow is metaphorical: the relationship becomes deeper or stronger.

items.example: We have been close friends since secondary school.
items.note: Close describes emotional intimacy, not physical distance.

items.example: Those two are special friends who have supported each other for years.
items.note: Special friends highlights a particular bond; it may have different connotations depending on context.

items.example: We discovered that we had several mutual friends.
items.note: Mutual friends are people known by both parties, not necessarily friends with each other.

items.pt: conhecido ocasional; pessoa com quem se tem pouco contato
items.example: I know her only as a casual acquaintance from work events.
items.note: An acquaintance is someone you know but may not be close to; casual makes the connection weaker.

items.word: have a good relationship with someone
items.pt: ter um bom relacionamento com alguém
items.example: He has a good relationship with his new manager.
items.note: Use have a relationship with, not have a relation with, when describing how well people get on.

items.example: We agreed to keep in contact after the training course.
items.note: Keep in contact means continue communicating; keep in touch is a very common alternative.

items.example: They still keep in touch even though they live in different countries.
items.note: Keep in touch and keep in contact have very similar meanings; touch is informal and common.

items.example: I lost contact with my school friends after moving abroad.
items.note: Lose contact means stop communicating with someone; contrast with keep in contact.

items.example: We lost touch for several years before meeting again.
items.note: Lose touch with someone is a natural alternative to lose contact with someone.

items.example: They fell madly in love while travelling together.
items.note: Madly intensifies falling in love and suggests intense romantic feelings, not insanity.

items.example: For them, it really was love at first sight.
items.note: The fixed expression describes an immediate romantic attraction at a first meeting.

items.example: She says her wife is the love of her life.
items.note: A strong expression for a person considered uniquely important in a romantic sense.

items.example: He cared for her but could not return her love.
items.note: Return someone’s love means reciprocate romantic feelings; love is the thing being returned.

items.example: He was desperately in love and could think of little else.
items.note: Desperately is an emotional intensifier; it does not always imply sadness or a desperate situation.

items.example: They decided to make a commitment to their relationship.
items.note: Make a commitment means formally or personally agree to a lasting obligation; often followed by to.

items.pt: aceitar um pedido de casamento; aceitar uma proposta
items.example: She happily accepted his proposal of marriage.
items.note: In the love-story context proposal means a marriage proposal, not a commercial offer.

items.example: They love each other unconditionally, even when they disagree.
items.note: Unconditionally means without attaching specific conditions to your affection.

items.pt: ter um caso extraconjugal; manter um relacionamento amoroso paralelo
items.example: The discovery that he had an affair ended their marriage.
items.note: In this context an affair means an intimate romantic or sexual relationship outside a committed partnership.

items.example: It can take time to fall in love with someone.
items.note: Fall in love is an idiomatic verb phrase for beginning to feel romantic love.

items.example: My best friend helped me prepare for the interview.
items.note: Best friend means someone especially close; the usual phrasing is my best friend or a best friend.

items.pt: amigo de longa data; amiga de longa data
items.example: I ran into an old friend from university at the station.
items.note: Old friend often means a friend you have known a long time, not necessarily someone elderly.

items.pt: amigo de infância; amiga de infância
items.example: A childhood friend visited us over the weekend.
items.note: Describes a friend from childhood, whether or not the friendship continues today.

items.example: A true friend will tell you when you need to hear something difficult.
items.note: True emphasises loyalty and sincerity rather than the length of the friendship.

items.example: I value our friendship and do not want a misunderstanding to damage it.
items.note: Value a friendship means regard it as important; the verb normally takes the relationship as object.

items.example: They chose to end their relationship on friendly terms.
items.note: End a relationship means bring it to a close; finish a relationship is less conventional in this sense.

items.example: The documentary explores a complicated family relationship across three generations.
items.note: A family relationship is a connection between family members; it does not necessarily imply romance.

items.example: She loved her partner deeply and was proud of their life together.
items.note: Deeply intensifies love and describes strength of feeling.

items.pt: mandar lembranças carinhosas a alguém; enviar carinho a alguém
items.example: Please send your grandmother my love when you visit her.
items.note: An affectionate message often conveyed through another person; my love is natural in this context.

items.word: hold out the hand of friendship
items.pt: estender a mão da amizade; oferecer reconciliação
items.example: After the disagreement, he held out the hand of friendship.
items.note: A metaphorical, slightly formal expression for offering friendship or reconciliation.

B · More than just good friends: love story, declarations of love, commitments and relationship choices
